report:
**Conclusion: the claim is supported, not false**—with an important qualification: tenofovir is *additional* prevention for women with high HBV DNA, alongside prompt infant hepatitis-B vaccination and usually hepatitis-B immune globulin (HBIG), not a substitute for infant immunization.

The biological rationale is strong: higher maternal HBV DNA at delivery is associated with failure of infant immunoprophylaxis. A pivotal randomized, open-label trial (Pan et al., *NEJM*, 2016) enrolled highly viremic mothers and began tenofovir disoproxil fumarate at 30–32 weeks. At delivery, 68% (66/97) of treated mothers versus 2% (2/100) of controls had HBV DNA below 200,000 IU/mL—evidence that the intervention substantially lowers the key transmission risk factor. The trial reported lower perinatal transmission with treatment.

This is reflected in major guidance. AASLD states that, when HBV DNA exceeds 200,000 IU/mL, antiviral therapy should start at 28–32 weeks to allow enough time to lower viral load. WHO’s 2024 HBV guidelines explicitly expanded eligibility for antiviral prophylaxis in pregnancy to prevent mother-to-child transmission.

The evidence is not that every HBV-positive pregnant person needs tenofovir: benefit is expected chiefly in high-viremia infection (commonly ≥200,000 IU/mL), and its absolute size depends on the quality/timing of newborn vaccination and HBIG. Questions remain about the optimal start date and long-term follow-up, but these do not overturn the conclusion that third-trimester tenofovir reduces transmission risk in the specified high-viral-load group.
